title: Rutherford's Gold Foil: Why the Plum-Pudding Atom Had to Go
intro: In 1909 Ernest Rutherford's team fired alpha particles at a sheet of gold foil thinner than a hair. You run the same experiment on a virtual bench. First you decide what the plum-pudding atom predicts. Then you collect the data, find the pattern in it, and rebuild the atom so the data makes sense.
introSteps: Do the pre-lab: three short questions, then place 100 alpha particles where you think they will land and give a reason. You get no feedback on the placement yet. The lab door stays locked until you finish.
Suit up, go through the door and step up to the bench (press E at it) to open the foil apparatus.
Run the plum-pudding model first, then the real gold foil. The detector records hit counts for every 10° of angle.
Find the pattern in your own counts, match each result to what it showed, then rebuild the atom with a nucleus.
Write the revision: a claim, evidence and reasoning that starts "The plum-pudding model fails because…" and cites a count from your own run. Hand-in opens after the minimum active lab time.
introKeys: Opens the foil apparatus, the detector table, and your answers.
Same thing: stand at the bench and press E.

theory.title: The plum-pudding atom (J. J. Thomson, 1904)
body: Thomson found that atoms contain tiny negative electrons, and atoms are neutral overall. So something positive must balance them. His picture: the positive charge is a soft, diffuse cloud filling the whole atom, with the electrons embedded in it like plums in a pudding.
In this picture nothing inside the atom is dense or concentrated. Every part of the atom is equally soft.

theory.title: The probe: alpha particles
body: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: two protons and two neutrons. It carries a positive charge and weighs about 7,300 times as much as an electron. Radioactive atoms shoot them out at about 5% of the speed of light.
Like charges repel. A fast, heavy, positive alpha particle is pushed sideways only when it passes close to a lot of positive charge. How hard it gets pushed tells you how concentrated that charge is.

theory.title: The detector
body: A zinc-sulfide screen flashes when an alpha particle hits it. Rutherford's team counted flashes at each angle, in a dark room, for hours. Here the detector counts for you and files every hit under its angle: 0–10°, 10–20°, and so on up to 180° (straight back toward the source).
Counts are the evidence. Your CER must quote some.

theory.title: Reading the counts
body: Add rows of the table to get a group: straight through is the 0–10° row, deflected is 10° through 90°, rebounded is anything past 90°. Divide a group by the total fired to get a fraction. A rare event is easier to say as "1 in N", where N is the total divided by the count.

options: A helium nucleus: positive and about 7,300 times heavier than an electron
A hydrogen atom with no electron
questions.explain: Two protons plus two neutrons, so it is positive and heavy. An electron is thousands of times too light to shove it much.

questions.q: In the plum-pudding model, where is the positive charge?
options: In a tiny hard core at the center
Spread evenly through the whole atom, with electrons embedded in it
On the outside surface of the atom
There is none; atoms have only electrons
questions.explain: Thomson's positive charge is diffuse, like pudding. No part of the atom is dense or concentrated.

questions.q: Which makes an alpha particle swerve more?
options: Passing near a lot of positive charge packed into a small space
Passing through a large soft region of weak positive charge
questions.explain: Repulsion grows steeply as distance shrinks, so a concentrated charge pushes harder than the same charge spread thin. That difference is the whole experiment.

placement.prompt: This is the plum-pudding gold atom. The foil is a few thousand atoms thick. Place where you think 100 alpha particles will land when fired at it, then give a one-sentence reason. The numbers must add to 100. There is no feedback on this part yet. You will see your prediction again after the real run.

data.q: What percent of your particles went straight through (the 0–10° row)?
data.hint: Look at the Real foil column of the detector table. Take the 0–10° count, divide by the total fired, and multiply by 100.

data.q: What percent were deflected (add the 10–20° row through the 80–90° row)?
data.hint: In the Real foil column, add every row from 10–20° down through 80–90°. Do not include the 0–10° row or anything past 90°. Divide by the total fired and multiply by 100.

data.q: Rebounds are the particles that came back past 90°. Rebounds were about 1 in how many fired?
data.hint: In the Real foil column, add every row from 90–100° to 180°. Divide the total fired by that sum to get N in "1 in N".

meanings.text: The atom is mostly empty space
The positive charge is concentrated in a tiny region
The center is heavy and dense

rows.hint: Most particles felt almost no push at all. What does that say about most of the volume of the atom?
A sharp swerve needs a big repulsive push. In the pudding model no part of the atom could do that. What would have to exist inside the atom?
Something that bounces back has hit something much heavier than itself, like a ball off a wall. What must the thing it hit be like?

challenge.prompt: Optional challenge: change one thing about the foil, then predict what happens to the number of large deflections before you run it.

change.text: Use a foil twice as thick (Gold, thickness 2)
Use a lighter target atom (Aluminum, thickness 1)

predictions.text: More particles are deflected sharply than with the normal gold foil

why.thick: A thicker foil gives each particle about twice as many chances to pass close to a nucleus, so about twice as many large deflections.
why.light: Aluminum nuclei have fewer protons (13 against 79), so each pushes less. Large deflections drop sharply.

postlab.prompt: Write the revision. Your claim must start with "The plum-pudding model fails because…". Support it with counts from your own real-foil run, then explain what each result showed about the atom.

reasoning: So the atom must be built like

checklist: My claim starts with "The plum-pudding model fails because".
I quote at least one count from my own run, with its angle range.
I say what the straight-through, large-deflection and rebound results each showed.
I say what the plum-pudding model predicted instead.

rubric.name: Claim
levels: States the failure but not why
States that the model cannot produce large deflections or rebounds

rubric.name: Evidence
levels: A count not tied to an angle range
Specific counts from own run, tied to angle ranges

rubric.name: Reasoning
levels: Links one result to a feature of the atom
Links all three results (empty space, concentrated charge, heavy core) and what the pudding predicted

quests.text: Put on goggles and an apron
quests.hint: Walk to the blue LOCKER (bottom left) and press E. Choose Put on for the goggles and the apron.

quests.text: Go through the door into the lab
quests.hint: The light on the DOOR turns green when you are geared up. Walk up through it.

quests.text: Step up to the bench to open the foil apparatus
quests.hint: Face the long BENCH and press E, or press N.

quests.text: Run the plum-pudding model (10,000 particles or more)
quests.hint: In the apparatus, keep the model on Plum pudding, press Fire, and let the counter pass 10,000.

quests.text: Run the real gold foil (20,000 particles)
quests.hint: The real foil unlocks once the plum-pudding run has 10,000 particles. Choose Real gold foil, then Fire.

quests.text: Answer the three data questions from your table
quests.hint: Open the Find the pattern section of the apparatus. Use the Real foil column of the detector table.

quests.text: Match each result to what it showed
quests.hint: Open the Match section of the apparatus. Choose a meaning for each result.

quests.text: Rebuild the atom with a nucleus and run it
quests.hint: Open the Rebuild section. Place the nucleus, then run your model. Compare it with the real foil.

quests.text: Write and submit your claim, evidence and reasoning
quests.hint: Press the Write CER button at the top. It opens once the apparatus work is finished.

quests.text: Challenge: change the foil, predict, then run it
quests.hint: Open the Challenge section. Pick a change, choose your prediction, then run it.
